essays.question: Some people say that children should learn ethics in school. Do you agree or disagree?

versions.text:
Some people say that ethics belongs at home, while others believe that schools should also teach children how to think about right and wrong. I agree that children should learn ethics at school, since it develops sound judgement and prepares them to live respectfully in a diverse society.

To begin with, ethics lessons teach children to reason about moral questions instead of merely following rules. Through discussions of real dilemmas, such as whether to report a friend who cheats or how to behave online, pupils learn to weigh evidence, consider other perspectives and justify their decisions. This capacity for independent reasoning is invaluable when they face pressure from peers or tempting shortcuts later in life. A student who has debated the fairness of sharing exam answers, for example, may be better prepared to resist the temptation to cheat.

Furthermore, ethics education promotes tolerance and responsible citizenship. Classrooms bring together children from different cultures and beliefs, and structured discussions help them to listen respectfully to views they do not share, which weakens prejudice and strengthens cooperation. Some argue that moral values should be taught by families, but parents differ widely in their approaches and many children receive little guidance at home. Schools can complement the family by offering a neutral setting in which pupils explore ideas without being told what to think, so the lessons need not clash with parental beliefs. These skills contribute to safer, more cooperative communities.

In conclusion, I am convinced that ethics should be taught in schools because it builds independent moral judgement and mutual respect, provided that lessons encourage open discussion rather than instruction.

essays.question: To what extent do you agree or disagree that technology should replace human teachers?

versions.text:
Advances in artificial intelligence and online platforms have led some people to suggest that technology could replace human teachers altogether. I strongly disagree with this view, since teachers provide motivation, guidance and human understanding that machines cannot offer, and an over-reliance on technology would deepen existing inequalities.

To begin with, good teaching depends on human relationships. A teacher can notice when a pupil is confused, anxious or struggling at home, adjust an explanation instantly and offer encouragement at the right moment. Teachers also act as role models, showing students how to argue respectfully, work with others and persevere when tasks are difficult. These qualities motivate learners in ways that software cannot reproduce. A shy pupil who finally speaks in class because a teacher patiently encouraged her, for example, gains a confidence that no automated system would have inspired.

Furthermore, replacing teachers with technology would widen inequality and carry practical risks. Not every family can afford a modern device or a reliable internet connection, so children from low-income or rural households would fall further behind. Devices also offer endless temptations such as games and social media, and learners who study alone on a screen miss the discipline and immediate feedback that a teacher provides. Admittedly, technology can help with marking and practice, but this is a reason to use it as a tool, not as a substitute.

In conclusion, technology should complement rather than replace teachers, because education relies on human motivation, understanding and fairness that machines cannot provide.

essays.question: Some people say that multilingual education is difficult for teachers. Do you agree or disagree?

versions.text:
Many schools around the world now teach in more than one language, and some people say that this is difficult for teachers. I largely agree, since multilingual education places considerable demands on staff, although these demands can be reduced with proper support.

To begin with, teachers must meet demanding language and preparation requirements. Staff must prepare materials in several languages, hold advanced language qualifications and adapt lessons for pupils at very different levels, all within the same working day. A science teacher required to deliver chemistry in a second language, for example, must first master the specialist vocabulary herself. Qualified teachers who are fluent in more than one language are also scarce, so schools may struggle to recruit enough of them, and existing staff face heavy workloads.

Furthermore, classrooms with mixed language levels complicate teaching and assessment. Some pupils speak the language of instruction fluently while others are only beginning, so teachers must explain concepts in several ways and design different tasks, which leaves less time for individual attention. Without extra training and support, this additional workload leaves many teachers exhausted and weakens the quality of lessons. However, the difficulty can be reduced. Governments can fund training and language courses for teachers, provide teaching assistants and shared materials, and limit class sizes. The educational and cultural benefits of multilingual education justify this investment, but it must not be left to individual teachers to cope alone.

In conclusion, multilingual education is difficult for teachers because of its workload and varied classrooms, but with training and resources the challenge is manageable.

essays.question: To what extent do you agree or disagree that school sports should be competitive?

versions.text:
Some schools emphasise competition in sport, while others prefer participation. I largely agree that school sports should be competitive, since competition builds resilience and teamwork, provided that no pupil is excluded or humiliated.

To begin with, competition teaches pupils how to handle both success and failure. Playing to win encourages effort, concentration and perseverance, while losing teaches children to accept disappointment and try again, which builds resilience that will serve them in exams and careers. Practising and improving for a match also shows that results come from patient, repeated effort rather than natural talent alone. A team that loses a match, for example, may learn to analyse its mistakes and train more effectively before the next game.

Furthermore, team competition fosters cooperation and a sense of belonging. Players must listen to others, accept roles and take shared responsibility for the result, and supporting the school team builds pride and community spirit. Competitive fixtures also motivate many pupils to keep fit. However, competition should be handled carefully. If only the strongest pupils play, weaker children may feel excluded or lose confidence, and excessive pressure to win can lead to conflict or injury. Schools should therefore offer teams at different levels, emphasise effort and fair play as much as victory, and provide non-competitive activities for those who prefer them, so that every child can enjoy sport in a way that suits them.

In conclusion, school sports should be competitive to a large extent because competition develops resilience and teamwork, but only when inclusion and fair play are protected.

essays.question: Some people believe that school libraries are outdated. Others disagree. Discuss both views and give your opinion.

versions.text:
Opinions are divided as to whether school libraries are outdated or remain valuable. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, critics argue that school libraries have lost their purpose in the digital age. Students can now find articles, e-books and videos on their phones in seconds, and online databases can serve thousands of users at once, at any hour and from any location, at a lower cost per user. Printed books quickly become out of date, and they require space, storage and staff that schools could use for laboratories or classrooms. Digital materials can also be updated instantly and searched in seconds. Many pupils therefore rarely visit the library, and money spent on shelves might be better invested in devices and online subscriptions.

On the other hand, supporters point out that libraries offer benefits that screens cannot. Books and databases are available free of charge, including to pupils who have no computer or internet at home, so libraries help to give everyone the same conditions and the same support. They provide a quiet space for study and encourage a reading habit, since children who browse shelves and choose their own books tend to enjoy reading more. Moreover, librarians help pupils to find reliable sources, a skill that becomes more important as online misinformation spreads. A student who cannot afford textbooks, for example, can still complete a research project by borrowing materials and using the library's databases.

To sum up, both positions have their merits; nevertheless, I believe that school libraries remain valuable, provided that they are modernised to combine books, digital resources and guidance on information.

essays.question: What are the causes of low participation in adult education? What solutions can be proposed?

versions.text:
The issue of low participation in adult education is a matter of growing concern. This essay will analyse the principal causes and propose realistic solutions.

Financial barriers play a substantial part in low participation in adult education. Fees, living costs and the loss of income while studying discourage many people from returning to education, particularly those from modest backgrounds. In addition, low awareness and motivation contribute to this problem. Where people see little connection between study and tangible rewards, or are held back by stereotypes and busy schedules, they simply do not engage. Working adults with family commitments are typical examples, as they must balance jobs, childcare and household tasks. A single parent who works two jobs, for example, has neither the money nor the energy for evening classes.

To address this issue, provision should be made more flexible and affordable. Subsidised fees, evening and online courses, and grants towards living costs allow people with limited money or time to participate without sacrificing their income. Barriers fall as a result, and participation rises among groups that were previously excluded. In addition, awareness campaigns and visible role models would change attitudes towards learning. Media campaigns, mentoring by successful adult learners and support from employers, such as paid study leave, show people that study leads to rewarding careers. Once these links become clear, motivation tends to follow, and workplaces can become partners in training.

In conclusion, low participation in adult education stems mainly from financial barriers and low awareness, but flexible and affordable provision and awareness campaigns offer a realistic way forward.

essays.question: How far do you think AI tutors will change education in the next 20 years? Support your answer with reasons.

versions.text:
AI tutors, programs that can explain topics, answer questions and set exercises at any hour, are improving rapidly. I believe that they will change education to a large extent over the next two decades, although human teachers will remain essential.

To begin with, AI tutors can give every learner individual attention that classrooms cannot. In a crowded classroom, a teacher rarely has time to adjust the pace for every child, whereas an AI system can identify a student's weaknesses, explain a concept in several ways and provide targeted practice immediately. Because such programs are available at any hour, learners no longer need to wait for the next lesson to get help. A pupil who is stuck on algebra at ten o'clock in the evening, for instance, can receive a patient explanation at once.

In addition, AI tutors will make good tutoring far cheaper and more widely available. Private tuition is expensive, so wealthy families have long enjoyed an advantage, whereas an AI tutor can reach pupils in remote villages or overcrowded schools at a fraction of the cost. Teachers, freed from repetitive marking and basic explanations, will be able to focus on discussion, creativity and emotional support. Nevertheless, the change will have limits. AI systems sometimes produce incorrect answers, raise privacy concerns and may encourage learners to depend on them instead of thinking independently, so human oversight will remain necessary.

In conclusion, AI tutors are likely to transform how students receive help and how teachers use their time, but their benefits depend on careful supervision and equal access.
